items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: The German alphabet, special sounds and spelling your name
explanation: German has 26 letters like English, plus ä, ö, ü and ß. The letter names are different, so learn them from the table. You need them to spell your name (buchstabieren), for example on the phone.

Some letters sound different from English. W sounds like English v (Wasser), V often sounds like f (Vater), and Z sounds like ts (Zahl). Ei sounds like English eye (heißen), and ie sounds like ee (Wiedersehen).

Ch, sch and tsch are different sounds. Sch sounds like English sh (Schule). Tsch sounds like English ch in church (Tschüs, Deutsch). Ä, ö and ü are changed vowels called Umlaute, and ß is a long ss sound (heißen).
To greet someone and ask their name, use Hallo, Wie heißt du? and Ich heiße ... To say goodbye, use Tschüs or Auf Wiedersehen.
original.rule_summary: Learn the letter names, spell names letter by letter, and keep tsch (like English ch) apart from sch (like English sh).

original.title: Hello and goodbye in German-speaking countries
original.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people often greet each other when they enter a small shop, a waiting room or a lift. A short Guten Tag! or Hallo! is polite. Many people use Guten Morgen! in the morning, and Guten Abend! in the evening. With friends and young people, Hallo! and Tschüs! are very common. With adults you do not know, people use Sie and often say Auf Wiedersehen! when they leave. In Switzerland you may hear different greetings, and in southern Germany and Austria people often say Servus or Grüß Gott. You do not need to use these yet, but it is nice to recognise them. Names are often spelled aloud on the phone, so the alphabet is very useful.
original.reflection_question: How do you usually greet people and say goodbye in your own language, and is it different for friends and for strangers?

original.task: Practise greeting and spelling your name out loud today, as you would in a real situation, for example on the phone or at a reception desk.
steps: Stand in front of a mirror or record yourself on your phone. Say: Hallo! Ich heiße ... (your name).

Say Guten Morgen!, Guten Tag! or Guten Abend! to match the time of day. Then say Tschüs! and Auf Wiedersehen! and listen carefully: tsch in Tschüs sounds like English "ch", not like "sh".

intro.title: The German alphabet, special sounds and spelling your name
explanation: German has 26 letters like English, plus ä, ö, ü and ß. The letter names are different, so learn them from the table. You need them to spell your name (buchstabieren), for example on the phone.

Some letters sound different from English. W sounds like English v (Wasser), V often sounds like f (Vater), and Z sounds like ts (Zahl). Ei sounds like English eye (heißen), and ie sounds like ee (Wiedersehen).

Ch, sch and tsch are different sounds. Sch sounds like English sh (Schule). Tsch sounds like English ch in church (Tschüs, Deutsch). Ä, ö and ü are changed vowels called Umlaute, and ß is a sharp s sound, like ss (heißen).
To greet someone and ask their name, use Hallo, Wie heißt du? and Ich heiße ... To say goodbye, use Tschüs or Auf Wiedersehen.
intro.rule_summary: Learn the letter names, spell names letter by letter, and keep tsch (like English ch) apart from sch (like English sh).

culture.title: Hello and goodbye in German-speaking countries
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people often greet each other when they enter a small shop, a waiting room or a lift. A short Guten Tag! or Hallo! is polite. Many people use Guten Morgen! in the morning, and Guten Abend! in the evening. With friends and young people, Hallo! and Tschüs! are very common. With adults you do not know, people use Sie and often say Auf Wiedersehen! when they leave. In Switzerland you may hear different greetings, and in southern Germany and Austria people often say Servus or Grüß Gott. You do not need to use these yet, but it is nice to recognise them. Names are often spelled aloud on the phone, so the alphabet is very useful.

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: Personal pronouns + sein; Ich heiße… / Ich bin… / Ich komme aus…
explanation: Personal pronouns tell us who is speaking or who we are talking about: ich (I), du (you, a friend), er (he), sie (she), wir (we), ihr (you, several friends), sie (they) and Sie (you, formal). The formal Sie always has a capital S.
The verb sein (to be) is irregular: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist. You use it for names, feelings and states: Ich bin Anna. Ich bin müde.
To say your name you can use heißen: Ich heiße Jonas. To say where you are from, use kommen + aus: Ich komme aus Deutschland.
To say how you feel, do not use 'Ich bin gut'. Say Mir geht es gut. The question is Wie geht es dir?
original.rule_summary: ich bin / du bist / er ist; Ich heiße… = my name; Ich komme aus… = where I am from; Mir geht es gut = I am fine.

items.label: Culture note

original.title: Du or Sie? Introducing yourself
original.note: In German-speaking countries, people choose between du and Sie. You use du with friends, family, children and fellow students. You use Sie with adults you do not know well, at work and in shops. Sie always has a capital S. When you are not sure, start with Sie. People often say their first name and sometimes their last name when they meet, for example "Ich heiße Anna Weber." Often people shake hands in a formal situation. In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, many people also say where they live or where they are from, but this is not required. If someone says "Wir können du sagen", it means you can now use du.
original.reflection_question: In your own country, how do you speak to a person you do not know well? Is there a difference like du and Sie?

intro.title: Personal pronouns + sein; Ich heiße… / Ich bin… / Ich komme aus…
explanation: Personal pronouns tell us who is speaking or who we are talking about: ich (I), du (you, a friend), er (he), sie (she), es (it), wir (we), ihr (you, several friends), sie (they) and Sie (you, formal). The formal Sie always has a capital S.
The verb sein (to be) is irregular: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist. You use it for names, feelings and states: Ich bin Anna. Ich bin müde.
To say your name you can use heißen: Ich heiße Jonas. To say where you are from, use kommen + aus: Ich komme aus Deutschland.
To say how you feel, do not use 'Ich bin gut'. Say Mir geht es gut. The question is Wie geht es dir?

culture.title: Du or Sie? Introducing yourself
culture.note: In German-speaking countries, people choose between du and Sie. You use du with friends, family, children and fellow students. You use Sie with adults you do not know well, at work and in shops. Sie always has a capital S. When you are not sure, start with Sie. People often say their first name and sometimes their last name when they meet, for example "Ich heiße Anna." Often people shake hands in a formal situation. In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, many people also say where they live or where they are from, but this is not required. If someone says "Wir können du sagen", it means you can now use du.

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: Numbers 0–100, phone numbers and age
explanation: Learn 0–12 as separate words: null, eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn, elf, zwölf. From 13 to 19 you say the small number plus -zehn: dreizehn, vierzehn. Watch the changes: sechzehn (not sechszehn) and siebzehn (not siebenzehn).

From 21 on, German says the small number FIRST: 21 = einundzwanzig, which is literally 'one-and-twenty'. You write it as one long word: ein + und + zwanzig. Note that 1 becomes ein- inside the word. The tens are zwanzig, dreißig, vierzig, fünfzig, sechzig, siebzig, achtzig, neunzig, hundert.
For a phone number, say each digit one by one: 0151 = null eins fünf eins. Take a short pause between groups. For age, German uses sein, not haben: Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt. Ask: Wie alt bist du?
original.rule_summary: 21–99 = small number + und + ten (einundzwanzig); phone numbers digit by digit; age = Ich bin … Jahre alt.

items.label: Culture note

original.title: Phone numbers in German-speaking countries
original.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people often say phone numbers in small groups of digits or in pairs, for example "fünf-vier" for 54. Some people say each digit alone. Zero is "null". When you give a number, people often repeat it to be sure. Mobile numbers are long, so it is normal to say them slowly. If you do not understand, you can say "Noch einmal, bitte." Many people also write the date and the house number after the street name: "Lindenstraße 12". The postcode (Postleitzahl) comes before the city name, for example "10115 Berlin". Germany uses the euro. Switzerland uses its own money, the Swiss franc.

intro.title: Numbers 0–100, phone numbers and age
explanation: Learn 0–12 as separate words: null, eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn, elf, zwölf. From 13 to 19 you say the small number plus -zehn: dreizehn, vierzehn. Watch the changes: sechzehn (not sechszehn) and siebzehn (not siebenzehn).

From 21 on, German says the small number FIRST: 21 = einundzwanzig, which is literally 'one-and-twenty'. You write it as one long word: ein + und + zwanzig. Note that 1 becomes ein- inside the word. The tens are zwanzig, dreißig, vierzig, fünfzig, sechzig, siebzig, achtzig, neunzig, hundert.
For a phone number, say each digit one by one: 0151 = null eins fünf eins. Take a short pause between groups. For age, German uses sein, not haben: Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt. Ask: Wie alt bist du?

explanation: German verbs in the dictionary form end in -en: wohnen, lernen, arbeiten, spielen. To use a verb, take off -en. What is left is the stem: wohn-, lern-, arbeit-, spiel-.
Then add an ending that matches the person: ich wohne, du wohnst, er wohnt, wir wohnen, ihr wohnt, sie wohnen. The verb changes, so you always need the right ending.
One present tense is enough: Ich wohne in Berlin means both 'I live in Berlin' and 'I am living in Berlin'.
If the stem ends in -t (arbeit-), add an extra e before -st and -t so it is easy to say: du arbeitest, er arbeitet, ihr arbeitet.
original.rule_summary: Stem + ending: -e (ich), -st (du), -t (er/sie/es, ihr), -en (wir, sie/Sie); with a stem ending in -t, add -e- before -st and -t.

items.label: Culture note

original.title: Living and studying in Germany
original.note: Many students in Germany do not live with their family. Some students live in a Wohnung with other students. This is called a WG (say: "Weh-Geh"), short for Wohngemeinschaft. Each person has their own Zimmer, and they share the kitchen and the bathroom. Other students live in a student residence or alone. Many cities have a big Universität, and students often come from different towns and countries. Students often ride a bike or take the bus to the Kurs. At many universities, students pay a small fee every semester, but often no high course fees. A WG is popular because rooms in big cities can be expensive.
original.reflection_question: Where do students usually live in your country: with family, alone, or with other students?

items.reason: The German letter W is said 'veh', so WG sounds 'Veh-Geh', not 'Weh-Geh'. Changed the hint.

culture.title: Living and studying in Germany
culture.note: Many students in Germany do not live with their family. Some students live in a Wohnung with other students. This is called a WG (say: "Veh-Geh"), short for Wohngemeinschaft. Each person has their own Zimmer, and they share the kitchen and the bathroom. Other students live in a student residence or alone. Many cities have a big Universität, and students often come from different towns and countries. Students often ride a bike or take the bus to the Kurs. At many universities, students pay a small fee every semester, but often no high course fees. A WG is popular because rooms in big cities can be expensive.

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: haben, der/die/das, ein/eine and the plural
explanation: Every German noun has a gender: masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das). The gender is not logical, so always learn a noun together with its article: der Tisch, die Lampe, das Buch.
'a' or 'an' is ein for der-words and das-words, and eine for die-words: ein Tisch, ein Buch, eine Lampe. Nouns always start with a capital letter.
The verb haben means 'to have'. It is irregular in du and er/sie/es: du hast, er hat. Example: Ich habe ein Handy.

In the plural, every noun uses die, whatever its gender: der Tisch, die Tische. The ending changes from noun to noun, so learn the plural too. Note: after haben, a der-word changes to einen (ich habe einen Stift). You will learn that later, so for now use haben with die-words and das-words.
original.rule_summary: Learn every noun with its article and plural; ein for der/das, eine for die; haben: ich habe, du hast, er/sie hat; plural always uses die.

'a' or 'an' is ein for der-words and das-words, and eine for die-words: ein Tisch, ein Buch, eine Lampe. Nouns always start with a capital letter.
The verb haben means 'to have'. It is irregular in du and er/sie/es: du hast, er hat. Example: Ich habe ein Handy.

In the plural, every noun uses die, whatever its gender: der Tisch, die Tische. The ending changes from noun to noun, so learn the plural too. Note: after haben, a der-word changes to einen (ich habe einen Stift). You will learn that later, so for now use haben with die-words and das-words.

intro.title: haben, der/die/das, ein/eine and the plural
explanation: Every German noun has a gender: masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das). The gender is not logical, so always learn a noun together with its article: der Tisch, die Lampe, das Buch.
'a' or 'an' is ein for der-words and das-words, and eine for die-words: ein Tisch, ein Buch, eine Lampe. Nouns always start with a capital letter.
The verb haben means 'to have'. It is irregular in du and er/sie/es: du hast, er hat. Example: Ich habe ein Handy.

In the plural, every noun uses die, whatever its gender: der Tisch, die Tische. The ending changes from noun to noun, so learn the plural too. Note: after haben, a der-word changes to einen (ich habe einen Stift). You will learn that later, so for now use haben with die-words and das-words.
intro.rule_summary: Learn every noun with its article and plural; ein for der/das, eine for die; haben: ich habe, du hast, er/sie hat; plural always uses die.

original.title: Asking questions: W-questions and yes/no questions
explanation: A W-question starts with a question word (wer, was, wo, woher, wie, wann). The verb comes straight after it, in second place: Wie heißt du?

The verb ending changes with the person. With du it ends in -st (du kommst). With ich it ends in -e (ich komme). With Sie (formal you) it ends in -en (Sie kommen).
original.rule_summary: W-question: question word + verb + subject. Yes/no question: verb + subject.

items.label: Culture note

original.title: Du or Sie when you meet someone
original.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people choose between du and Sie when they ask questions. Children, family, friends and most students say du to each other. Adults who do not know each other well, for example in a shop, in an office or at work, usually say Sie. With Sie, the question sounds like this: Wie heißen Sie? Woher kommen Sie? Sie always has a capital S. If you are not sure, start with Sie. Often the other person then says: Wir können du sagen. That means you can both use du. At a language course, people often ask the same first questions: name, country, city and languages. It is normal and friendly to ask them.
original.reflection_question: In your country, how do people ask each other's name when they meet for the first time? Is there a difference between friends and strangers?

intro.title: Asking questions: W-questions and yes/no questions
explanation: A W-question starts with a question word (wer, was, wo, woher, wie, wann). The verb comes straight after it, in second place: Wie heißt du?
A yes/no question has no question word. The verb comes first: Wohnst du in Berlin? You answer with Ja or Nein.

culture.title: Du or Sie when you meet someone
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people choose between du and Sie when they ask questions. Children, family, friends and most students say du to each other. Adults who do not know each other well, for example in a shop, in an office or at work, usually say Sie. With Sie, the question sounds like this: Wie heißen Sie? Woher kommen Sie? Sie always has a capital S. If you are not sure, start with Sie. Often the other person then says: Wir können du sagen. That means you can both use du. At a language course, people often ask the same first questions: name, country, city and languages. It is normal and friendly to ask them.

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: The verb always comes second
explanation: In a German statement, the conjugated verb always stands in position 2. Position 1 can be the subject (Ich lerne heute Deutsch.) or something else, such as a time word (Heute lerne ich Deutsch.).
Position 1 can be one word or a short group of words that belong together, for example 'Am Montag' or 'Im Sommer'. Count the whole group as one position. The verb comes right after it.
If you put a time word first, the subject moves behind the verb. So it is 'Heute lerne ich', not 'Heute ich lerne'. The meaning stays the same, only the focus changes.
Use am for days (am Montag) and im for months and seasons (im Mai, im Sommer).
original.rule_summary: Position 1 (subject or time) + verb in position 2 + the rest: Heute lerne ich Deutsch.

items.reason: Accurate, simple explanation of verb-second order.

final.title: The verb always comes second
explanation: In a German statement, the conjugated verb always stands in position 2. Position 1 can be the subject (Ich lerne heute Deutsch.) or something else, such as a time word (Heute lerne ich Deutsch.).

intro.title: The verb always comes second
explanation: In a German statement, the conjugated verb always stands in position 2. Position 1 can be the subject (Ich lerne heute Deutsch.) or something else, such as a time word (Heute lerne ich Deutsch.).
Position 1 can be one word or a short group of words that belong together, for example 'Am Montag' or 'Im Sommer'. Count the whole group as one position. The verb comes right after it.
If you put a time word first, the subject moves behind the verb. So it is 'Heute lerne ich', not 'Heute ich lerne'. The meaning stays the same, only the focus changes.
Use am for days (am Montag) and im for months and seasons (im Mai, im Sommer).
intro.rule_summary: Position 1 (subject or time) + verb in position 2 + the rest: Heute lerne ich Deutsch.

examples.note: Heute is in position 1, the verb lerne is in position 2, and ich comes after the verb.

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: Telling the time, and 'um' and 'am' for when
explanation: To ask the time, say 'Wie spät ist es?' To answer, say 'Es ist ... Uhr.' For example: 'Es ist drei Uhr.' For one o'clock, say 'ein Uhr' (not 'eins Uhr').

There are two ways to say the time. In everyday speech (informal) we use 'nach' (past), 'vor' (to), 'Viertel' (quarter) and 'halb' (half). On trains, at work and in announcements (formal) we use the 24-hour clock: 'Es ist fünfzehn Uhr dreißig.' Careful: 'halb vier' means 3:30, half an hour on the way to four.

To say when you do something, use 'um' with a clock time: 'um sieben Uhr' (at seven o'clock). Use 'am' with a part of the day or a day of the week: 'am Morgen', 'am Abend', 'am Montag'. The question is 'Wann ...?' (When ...?). The verb stays in second place: 'Anna frühstückt um sieben Uhr.' / 'Um sieben Uhr frühstückt Anna.'

items.label: Culture note

original.title: Clocks and being on time
original.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, punctuality is important. People usually arrive on time for work, school, doctor's appointments and trains. If you will be late, it is polite to call or write a message. In writing, on timetables and in formal situations, people often use the 24-hour clock, for example 14:30. In everyday speech, many people use the 12-hour clock and say 'halb drei'. Be careful: halb drei does not mean 2:30 in English thinking. It means half way to three, so it is 2:30. Many people also say 'Viertel nach' or 'Viertel vor' for quarter past and quarter to. Listening to how people say the time at the station or on the radio is great practice.
original.reflection_question: How important is being on time in your country, and what is different from what you read here?

items.reason: The sentence 'halb drei does not mean 2:30 ... so it is 2:30' contradicted itself. Rewrote it to contrast halb drei with British 'half three'.

final.title: Clocks and being on time

In everyday speech, many people use the 12-hour clock and say 'halb drei'. Be careful: halb drei does not mean 'half past three' (like 'half three' in British English). intro.title: Telling the time, and 'um' and 'am' for when
explanation: To ask the time, say 'Wie spät ist es?' To answer, say 'Es ist ... Uhr.' For example: 'Es ist drei Uhr.' For one o'clock, say 'ein Uhr' (not 'eins Uhr').

There are two ways to say the time. In everyday speech (informal) we use 'nach' (past), 'vor' (to), 'Viertel' (quarter) and 'halb' (half). On trains, at work and in announcements (formal) we use the 24-hour clock: 'Es ist fünfzehn Uhr dreißig.' Careful: 'halb vier' means 3:30, half an hour on the way to four.

To say when you do something, use 'um' with a clock time: 'um sieben Uhr' (at seven o'clock). Use 'am' with a part of the day or a day of the week: 'am Morgen', 'am Abend', 'am Montag'. The question is 'Wann ...?' (When ...?). The verb stays in second place: 'Anna frühstückt um sieben Uhr.' / 'Um sieben Uhr frühstückt Anna.'

culture.title: Clocks and being on time
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, punctuality is important. People usually arrive on time for work, school, doctor's appointments and trains. If you will be late, it is polite to call or write a message. In writing, on timetables and in formal situations, people often use the 24-hour clock, for example 14:30. In everyday speech, many people use the 12-hour clock and say 'halb drei'. Be careful: halb drei does not mean 'half past three' (like 'half three' in British English). It means half way to three, so it is 2:30. Many people also say 'Viertel nach' or 'Viertel vor' for quarter past and quarter to. Listening to how people say the time at the station or on the radio is great practice.

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: du or Sie? Small talk in a café
explanation: German has two words for 'you'. Use du with friends, family, children and other students. Use Sie with adults you do not know well, with teachers, at work and in shops. When in doubt, start with Sie.

The verb changes with du and Sie. With du the verb ends in -st: du heißt, du kommst. With Sie the verb ends in -en: Sie heißen, Sie kommen. The formal Sie always has a capital S. The verb sein is special: du bist, Sie sind.
A short small-talk dialogue uses what you already know: greeting, name, origin, how are you, thank you. Keep the same form (du or Sie) in the whole dialogue.
original.rule_summary: du + verb ending -st (friends); Sie + verb ending -en (formal, capital S); keep one form in a whole dialogue.

original.title: Coffee and cake in a German café
original.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, many people enjoy coffee and cake in the afternoon. Friends often meet in a café and stay for a long time. When you come into a small café, you can ask "Ist hier noch frei?" before you sit at a table with other people. Often you pay at the table: the waiter or waitress comes and asks "Zusammen oder getrennt?" (together or separately?). Many people also add a small tip, for example by rounding up the bill. With waiters and waitresses you do not know, use Sie. Among friends, use du.

intro.title: du or Sie? Small talk in a café
explanation: German has two words for 'you'. Use du with friends, family, children and other students. Use Sie with adults you do not know well, with teachers, at work and in shops. When in doubt, start with Sie.

The verb changes with du and Sie. With du the verb usually ends in -st: du kommst, du wohnst (but du heißt, because the stem already ends in ß). With Sie the verb ends in -en: Sie heißen, Sie kommen. The formal Sie always has a capital S. The verb sein is special: du bist, Sie sind.
A short small-talk dialogue uses what you already know: greeting, name, origin, how are you, thank you. Keep the same form (du or Sie) in the whole dialogue.
intro.rule_summary: du + verb ending -st (friends); Sie + verb ending -en (formal, capital S); keep one form in a whole dialogue.

culture.title: Coffee and cake in a German café
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, many people enjoy coffee and cake in the afternoon. Friends often meet in a café and stay for a long time. When you come into a small café, you can ask "Ist hier noch frei?" before you sit at a table with other people. Often you pay at the table: the waiter or waitress comes and asks "Zusammen oder getrennt?" (together or separately?). Many people also add a small tip, for example by rounding up the bill. With waiters and waitresses you do not know, use Sie. Among friends, use du.

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: Introducing yourself: present tense, W-questions and verb in second place
explanation: Regular German verbs lose -en from the infinitive and add an ending for each person: ich komme, du kommst, er/sie kommt, wir kommen, ihr kommt, sie/Sie kommen. The verbs sein (to be) and haben (to have) are irregular, so learn their forms by heart.
W-questions start with a question word (Wie, Woher, Wo, Wer, Was) and then the verb: Wie heißt du? Woher kommst du? Wo wohnst du?

In a statement the conjugated verb is always in second position. The first position can be the subject (Ich wohne in Bonn.) or another element such as Jetzt (Jetzt wohne ich in Bonn.). The verb stays second and the subject moves behind it.
To ask about age, use sein: Wie alt bist du? Ich bin 20 (Jahre alt).
original.rule_summary: Verb endings follow the person; sein and haben are irregular; in statements and W-questions the conjugated verb stands in second position (in W-questions right after the question word).

original.title: Du or Sie? Introducing yourself
original.note: In German-speaking countries, people usually shake hands when they meet for the first time in a formal situation, and they often say their name: "Guten Tag, ich heiße Anna Weber." With adults you do not know, at work or in shops, you use Sie and often the last name, for example "Frau Weber" or "Herr Weber". Friends, family, children and many fellow students say du and use first names. Among young people and in many workplaces, people switch to du quickly, but it is polite to wait until the other person offers it. When in doubt, start with Sie. A small, friendly "Freut mich!" is a good answer after you hear someone's name.
original.reflection_question: How do people in your country greet each other when they meet for the first time, and does your language also have a formal and an informal "you"?

intro.title: Introducing yourself: present tense, W-questions and verb in second place
explanation: Regular German verbs lose -en from the infinitive and add an ending for each person: ich komme, du kommst, er/sie kommt, wir kommen, ihr kommt, sie/Sie kommen. The verbs sein (to be) and haben (to have) are irregular, so learn their forms by heart.
W-questions start with a question word (Wie, Woher, Wo, Wer, Was) and then the verb: Wie heißt du? Woher kommst du? Wo wohnst du?

In a statement the conjugated verb is always in second position. The first position can be the subject (Ich wohne in Bonn.) or another element such as Jetzt (Jetzt wohne ich in Bonn.). The verb stays second and the subject moves behind it.
To ask about age, use sein: Wie alt bist du? Ich bin 20 (Jahre alt).
intro.rule_summary: Verb endings follow the person; sein and haben are irregular; in statements and W-questions the conjugated verb stands in second position (in W-questions right after the question word).

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: Articles: Nominativ and Akkusativ
explanation: Every German noun has a gender: masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das). In the plural, all nouns use die. The article shows the gender, so learn each noun together with its article: der Vater, die Mutter, das Kind.

The Nominativ is the case of the subject, the person or thing that does the action. It is also used after sein: Der Vater ist nett. Das ist ein Bruder. The Akkusativ is the case of the direct object, for example after haben (I have) or sehen (I see): Ich habe einen Bruder.
Only the masculine changes from Nominativ to Akkusativ: der becomes den, and ein becomes einen. Feminine (die, eine), neuter (das, ein) and plural (die) stay the same.
original.rule_summary: Nominativ = subject (and after sein); Akkusativ = object (after haben, sehen): only masculine changes: der → den, ein → einen.

items.label: Culture note

original.title: Family in German-speaking countries
original.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, many people live in small households: a single person, a couple, or parents with one or two children. Grandparents often live in another town, so families often meet on weekends, on birthdays and at holidays. Many families have coffee and cake together on Sunday afternoon. When Germans talk about the family, they often say die Familie for parents and children, and die Verwandten for relatives such as Onkel, Tante, Cousin and Cousine. Families are very different, and many children also have step-parents or live with one parent. In everyday speech, many people say Oma and Opa for grandparents, and Mama and Papa for parents.

intro.title: Articles: Nominativ and Akkusativ
explanation: Every German noun has a gender: masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das). In the plural, all nouns use die. The article shows the gender, so learn each noun together with its article: der Vater, die Mutter, das Kind.

The Nominativ is the case of the subject, the person or thing that does the action. It is also used after sein: Der Vater ist nett. Das ist ein Bruder. The Akkusativ is the case of the direct object, for example after haben (I have) or sehen (I see): Ich habe einen Bruder.
Only the masculine changes from Nominativ to Akkusativ: der becomes den, and ein becomes einen. Feminine (die, eine), neuter (das, ein) and plural (die) stay the same.
intro.rule_summary: Nominativ = subject (and after sein); Akkusativ = object (after haben, sehen): only masculine changes: der → den, ein → einen.

culture.title: Family in German-speaking countries
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, many people live in small households: a single person, a couple, or parents with one or two children. Grandparents often live in another town, so families often meet on weekends, on birthdays and at holidays. Many families have coffee and cake together on Sunday afternoon. When Germans talk about the family, they often say die Familie for parents and children, and die Verwandten for relatives such as Onkel, Tante, Cousin and Cousine. Families are very different, and many children also have step-parents or live with one parent. In everyday speech, many people say Oma and Opa for grandparents, and Mama and Papa for parents.

original.title: Saying no: nicht or kein?
explanation: German has two main words for negation. Use kein (a form of ein) to negate a noun that has ein/eine or no article at all: Ich habe einen Balkon. → Ich habe keinen Balkon. Kein takes the endings of ein: kein, keine, keinen.
Use nicht for everything else: to negate a verb, an adjective, or a noun with a definite article (der, die, das) or with mein/dein: Das Bad ist nicht groß. Lena kauft den Tisch nicht.

Nicht usually goes at the end of a short sentence. Before an adjective it stands directly in front of it: nicht groß. Kein stands right before the noun and changes like ein (masculine accusative: keinen).
original.rule_summary: ein-noun or no article → kein/keine/keinen + noun; verb, adjective or der/die/das-noun → nicht.

original.title: Renting a flat in Germany
original.note: Many people in Germany, Austria and Switzerland rent their home instead of buying it. The monthly rent is called die Miete. You often see two prices: Kaltmiete (rent only) and Warmmiete (rent plus costs such as heating). Some empty flats come without a kitchen, so tenants bring or buy their own. In many buildings, names are written next to the doorbell at the front door. Most buildings also have quiet hours, often at night and on Sundays, when people try not to make noise. Rules differ between buildings, so it is polite to check the house rules (die Hausordnung).

intro.title: Saying no: nicht or kein?
explanation: German has two main words for negation. Use kein (a form of ein) to negate a noun that has ein/eine or no article at all: Ich habe einen Balkon. → Ich habe keinen Balkon. Kein takes the endings of ein: kein, keine, keinen.
Use nicht for everything else: to negate a verb, an adjective, or a noun with a definite article (der, die, das) or with mein/dein: Das Bad ist nicht groß. Lena kauft den Tisch nicht.

Nicht usually goes at the end of a short sentence. Before an adjective it stands directly in front of it: nicht groß. Kein stands right before the noun and changes like ein (masculine accusative: keinen).
intro.rule_summary: ein-noun or no article → kein/keine/keinen + noun; verb, adjective or der/die/das-noun → nicht.

culture.title: Renting a flat in Germany
culture.note: Many people in Germany, Austria and Switzerland rent their home instead of buying it. The monthly rent is called die Miete. You often see two prices: Kaltmiete (rent only) and Warmmiete (rent plus costs such as heating). Some empty flats come without a kitchen, so tenants bring or buy their own. In many buildings, names are written next to the doorbell at the front door. Most buildings also have quiet hours, often at night and on Sundays, when people try not to make noise. Rules differ between buildings, so it is polite to check the house rules (die Hausordnung).

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: Modal verbs I: können, müssen, wollen, dürfen
explanation: Modal verbs are small helper verbs that add a meaning to another verb. können = can / to be able to, müssen = must / to have to, wollen = to want to, dürfen = may / to be allowed to. Example: Ich kann Suppe kochen = I can cook soup.

The modal verb is conjugated and stands in second position. The main verb stays in the infinitive and goes to the very end of the sentence: Anna will Tee trinken. In a question the modal verb comes first: Darf ich ein Glas Wasser haben?

Modal verbs are irregular in the singular. Ich and er/sie/es have no ending and are always the same (ich kann, er kann). The vowel often changes in the singular: können → kann, müssen → muss, wollen → will, dürfen → darf. The wir and sie/Sie forms are the same as the infinitive.
When ordering politely, Germans often use möchte (would like) instead of will. Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. sounds friendly, while Ich will einen Kaffee. sounds blunt.
original.rule_summary: Modal verb (conjugated) in position 2 + main verb in the infinitive at the end: Ich kann Suppe kochen.

original.title: Paying at the table
original.note: In many German restaurants, you do not pay at the counter. You stay at your table and say to the waiter or waitress: "Ich möchte bezahlen, bitte." Then the person comes to your table with the bill. Often the server asks: "Zusammen oder getrennt?" This means: together or separately? Paying separately is normal and not rude. Many people also add a small tip. They often round up the amount, for example from 18 euros to 20 euros, and say "Stimmt so." Before the meal, people often say "Guten Appetit!" to each other. In many places you can also ask for tap water, but it is not always free, and some restaurants bring only bottled water. Look at the Speisekarte for prices.

intro.title: Modal verbs I: können, müssen, wollen, dürfen
explanation: Modal verbs are small helper verbs that add a meaning to another verb. können = can / to be able to, müssen = must / to have to, wollen = to want to, dürfen = may / to be allowed to. Example: Ich kann Suppe kochen = I can cook soup.

The modal verb is conjugated and stands in second position. The main verb stays in the infinitive and goes to the very end of the sentence: Anna will Tee trinken. In a question the modal verb comes first: Darf ich ein Glas Wasser haben?

Modal verbs are irregular in the singular. Ich and er/sie/es have no ending and are always the same (ich kann, er kann). The vowel often changes in the singular: können → kann, müssen → muss, wollen → will, dürfen → darf. The wir and sie/Sie forms are the same as the infinitive.
When ordering politely, Germans often use möchte (would like) instead of will. Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. sounds friendly, while Ich will einen Kaffee. sounds blunt.
intro.rule_summary: Modal verb (conjugated) in position 2 + main verb in the infinitive at the end: Ich kann Suppe kochen.

original.title: Separable verbs: the prefix goes to the end
explanation: Many German verbs have a prefix that can separate, such as auf-stehen, ein-kaufen, an-rufen and fern-sehen. In the dictionary and after words like müssen you see the whole verb: aufstehen.
In a normal statement or question, the verb stem takes the ending and stays in position 2 (or first in a question). The prefix jumps to the very end of the sentence: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
Other information (time, place, objects) goes between the verb and the prefix: Anna kauft heute im Supermarkt ein.
Not every verb with a prefix separates. Frühstücken is just one verb, so it does not split: Ich frühstücke um acht Uhr.
original.rule_summary: Main clause: conjugated stem in position 2, separable prefix at the end: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.

original.focus: Stressed prefixes in separable verbs, and the sounds au, ei and äu
original.explanation: In separable verbs the prefix is stressed: AUFstehen, EINkaufen, ANrufen. In the sentence the stressed prefix at the end is clearly heard. Also: au sounds like English "ow" in "now", ei like "eye", and äu like "oy" in "boy".

words.hint: AUF-shte-en: stress on AUF, au = ow, st at the start of a stem sounds like sht
EIN-kow-fen: ei = eye, au = ow, stress on EIN
FERN-zay-en: s before a vowel is like English z
AP-hoh-len: b at the end of a syllable sounds like p
AUF-vakh-en: w = English v, ch like a soft hiss in the throat

original.title: Daily rhythm in German-speaking countries
original.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, many people start work or school fairly early, often between seven and nine in the morning. Many people eat a quick breakfast at home, for example bread with cheese or jam. The main hot meal is often at midday, but many adults who work have a lighter lunch in a short break and eat a warm meal in the evening. The evening meal is often simpler and is sometimes called Abendbrot, which refers to bread with cold food. Punctuality is valued: arriving on time for an appointment or a course is normal and polite. If you will be late, it is common to call or write a message. Shops often close in the evening, and in many places they are closed on Sundays, so people often go shopping on Saturday or during the week.

intro.title: Separable verbs: the prefix goes to the end
explanation: Many German verbs have a prefix that can separate, such as auf-stehen, ein-kaufen, an-rufen and fern-sehen. In the dictionary and after words like müssen you see the whole verb: aufstehen.
In a normal statement or question, the verb stem takes the ending and stays in position 2 (or first in a question). The prefix jumps to the very end of the sentence: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
Other information (time, place, objects) goes between the verb and the prefix: Anna kauft heute im Supermarkt ein.
Not every verb with a prefix separates. Frühstücken is just one verb, so it does not split: Ich frühstücke um acht Uhr.
intro.rule_summary: Main clause: conjugated stem in position 2, separable prefix at the end: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.

pronunciation.focus: Stressed prefixes in separable verbs, and the sounds au, ei and äu
pronunciation.explanation: In separable verbs the prefix is stressed: AUFstehen, EINkaufen, ANrufen. In the sentence the stressed prefix at the end is clearly heard. Also: au sounds like English "ow" in "now", ei like "eye", and äu like "oy" in "boy".

words.hint: AUF-shte-en: stress on AUF, au = ow, st at the start of a stem sounds like sht
EIN-kow-fen: ei = eye, au = ow, stress on EIN
FERN-zay-en: s before a vowel is like English z
AP-hoh-len: b at the end of a syllable sounds like p
AUF-vakh-en: w = English v, ch like a soft hiss in the throat

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: Dative articles: dem, der, dem, den
explanation: In German the noun's job in the sentence changes the article. After some small words (prepositions) like mit, bei, von, zu and aus, and after the verb geben (to give) for the person who receives something, you use the dative case.
The dative articles are: masculine dem, feminine der, neuter dem, plural den. Compare: der Verkäufer becomes dem Verkäufer, die Karte becomes der Karte, das Geld becomes dem Geld.
In the plural, the noun usually also gets an -n: die Kinder becomes mit den Kindern. If the plural already ends in -n (die Kunden), nothing is added.
The same pattern works with ein and kein: einem, einer, einem. Some short forms are very common: bei + dem = beim, zu + dem = zum, zu + der = zur, von + dem = vom.
original.rule_summary: Dative: der → dem, die → der, das → dem, plural die → den (+n); ein → einem, eine → einer; used after mit, bei, von, zu, aus and for the person who receives (geben).

original.title: Shopping in Germany
original.note: In Germany many people buy bread at a Bäcker and fresh fruit and vegetables at a market or in a supermarket. Most shops close on Sundays, so people often shop on Saturday. At the supermarket checkout, you usually put your things on the belt and pack them yourself, often in your own Tasche, because plastic bags usually cost extra. Many shops accept a Karte, but some small bakeries and market stalls prefer cash, so it is useful to ask: Kann ich mit der Karte bezahlen? Greeting the Verkäufer or the Verkäuferin with Guten Tag and saying Bitte and Danke is polite and normal.

intro.title: Dative articles: dem, der, dem, den
explanation: In German the noun's job in the sentence changes the article. After some small words (prepositions) like mit, bei, von, zu and aus, and after the verb geben (to give) for the person who receives something, you use the dative case.
The dative articles are: masculine dem, feminine der, neuter dem, plural den. Compare: der Verkäufer becomes dem Verkäufer, die Karte becomes der Karte, das Geld becomes dem Geld.
In the plural, the noun usually also gets an -n: die Kinder becomes mit den Kindern. If the plural already ends in -n (die Kunden), nothing is added.
The same pattern works with ein and kein: einem, einer, einem. Some short forms are very common: bei + dem = beim, zu + dem = zum, zu + der = zur, von + dem = vom.
intro.rule_summary: Dative: der → dem, die → der, das → dem, plural die → den (+n); ein → einem, eine → einer; used after mit, bei, von, zu, aus and for the person who receives (geben).

culture.title: Shopping in Germany
culture.note: In Germany many people buy bread at a Bäcker and fresh fruit and vegetables at a market or in a supermarket. Most shops close on Sundays, so people often shop on Saturday. At the supermarket checkout, you usually put your things on the belt and pack them yourself, often in your own Tasche, because plastic bags usually cost extra. Many shops accept a Karte, but some small bakeries and market stalls prefer cash, so it is useful to ask: Kann ich mit der Karte bezahlen? Greeting the Verkäufer or the Verkäuferin with Guten Tag and saying Bitte and Danke is polite and normal.
culture.reflection_question: How are shops where you live different from this? Do you usually pay with Geld or with a Karte?

mission.title: Shopping words around you
mission.task: Practise the shopping phrases in real life or by speaking aloud, and use the dative article after mit and bei.
steps: Next time you are in a shop, a bakery or at a market, look for three things and say their names in German, for example: der Apfel, das Brot, die Tasche.
Say aloud or write three short sentences with the dative, for example: Ich bezahle mit der Karte. Ich kaufe Brot beim Bäcker. Ich gebe dem Verkäufer das Geld.
Practise the phrases Ich möchte ein Brot, bitte. and Was kostet das? by speaking them aloud as if you were in a shop. If you are in a German-speaking place, try one phrase in a real shop.
mission.report_prompt: Write the three things you found, your three dative sentences, and which phrase you practised or used.
success_check: I named three shopping items in German.
I wrote three sentences with dem, der or einem.
I said Was kostet das? or Kann ich mit der Karte bezahlen? aloud.

original.title: Verbs with the dative: helfen, gefallen, gehören, danken
explanation: Most German verbs take an accusative object (Ich sehe dich). A few important verbs take a dative object instead: helfen (to help), gefallen (to please / to be liked), gehören (to belong to) and danken (to thank). The person after them is in the dative: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen.

gefallen works differently from English. In Die Jacke gefällt mir the jacket is the subject and I am the dative object. Word for word it means "The jacket pleases me", so the verb agrees with the thing: Die Jacke gefällt mir, Die Schuhe gefallen mir.
gehören works the same way: Die Mütze gehört ihm. To ask about the owner, use Wem? (to whom): Wem gehört die Tasche? With names, the name simply stays the same: Die Jacke gehört Lena.
original.rule_summary: helfen, gefallen, gehören and danken are followed by the dative: Ich helfe dir. Die Hose gefällt mir. Die Mütze gehört ihm. Ich danke Ihnen.

original.title: Buying clothes in Germany
original.note: In Germany, many people buy clothes in shops, in markets and online. In shops, staff often say Kann ich Ihnen helfen? and you can answer Danke, ich schaue nur. Clothes sizes are numbers, for example 38 or 42, and often letters like S, M and L. Most shops let you try things on in a changing room, die Umkleidekabine. If you buy something and keep the receipt, der Kassenbon, you can often bring it back within a certain time, but each shop has its own rules, so ask at the till. In many places people like practical clothes for changing weather, such as a jacket for rain. Being polite helps: say Guten Tag when you enter and Danke and Tschüs when you leave.

intro.title: Verbs with the dative: helfen, gefallen, gehören, danken
explanation: Most German verbs take an accusative object (Ich sehe dich). A few important verbs take a dative object instead: helfen (to help), gefallen (to please / to be liked), gehören (to belong to) and danken (to thank). The person after them is in the dative: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen.

gefallen works differently from English. In Die Jacke gefällt mir the jacket is the subject and I am the dative object. Word for word it means "The jacket pleases me", so the verb agrees with the thing: Die Jacke gefällt mir, Die Schuhe gefallen mir.
gehören works the same way: Die Mütze gehört ihm. To ask about the owner, use Wem? (to whom): Wem gehört die Tasche? With names, the name simply stays the same: Die Jacke gehört Lena.
intro.rule_summary: helfen, gefallen, gehören and danken are followed by the dative: Ich helfe dir. Die Hose gefällt mir. Die Mütze gehört ihm. Ich danke Ihnen.

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: Possessive articles: mein, dein, sein, ihr
explanation: A possessive article shows who something belongs to: mein Bus (my bus), dein Park (your park). The stem depends on the owner: ich = mein, du = dein, er/es = sein, sie = ihr, wir = unser, ihr = euer, Sie = Ihr.
The ending depends on the noun that follows: its gender, its number and its case. The endings are the same as for ein/eine/ein (and kein): mein Bahnhof, meine Straße, mein Haus, meine Freunde.

In the nominative (the subject) the masculine and neuter forms have no ending. In the accusative (the direct object) only the masculine changes: Ich sehe meinen Bahnhof. In the dative (after mit, bei, zu, in for where?) the endings are -em, -er, -em, -en: mit meinem Bus, mit meiner Freundin.
In the dative plural the noun also usually gets -n: bei meinen Eltern. Remember: sein = his, ihr = her. The owner decides the stem, not the noun.
original.rule_summary: Stem = owner (mein, dein, sein, ihr); ending = noun's gender and case, like ein: Nom mein/meine/mein, Akk meinen/meine/mein, Dat meinem/meiner/meinem.

final.title: Possessive articles: mein, dein, sein, ihr
explanation: A possessive article shows who something belongs to: mein Bus (my bus), dein Park (your park). The stem depends on the owner: ich = mein, du = dein, er/es = sein, sie = ihr, wir = unser, ihr = euer, Sie = Ihr.
The ending depends on the noun that follows: its gender, its number and its case. The endings are the same as for ein/eine/ein (and kein): mein Bahnhof, meine Straße, mein Haus, meine Freunde.

In the nominative (the subject) the masculine and neuter forms have no ending. In the accusative (the direct object) only the masculine changes: Ich sehe meinen Bahnhof. In the dative (after mit, bei, zu, in for where?) the endings are -em, -er, -em, -en: mit meinem Bus, mit meiner Freundin.
In the dative plural the noun also usually gets -n: bei meinen Eltern. Remember: sein = his, ihr = her. The owner decides the stem, not the noun.
final.rule_summary: Stem = owner (mein, dein, sein, ihr); ending = noun's gender and case, like ein: Nom mein/meine/mein, Akk meinen/meine/mein, Dat meinem/meiner/meinem.

original.note: In many German, Austrian and Swiss cities, people use buses, trams, trains and bicycles every day. You often buy a ticket at a machine or in an app, and at many stops you must validate it before you ride, for example in some cities. Cities usually have a Bahnhof in the centre, and many streets have bike lanes. Many people live in flats, so they often tell friends their street and house number, for example: Ich wohne in der Bahnhofstraße 5. Shops such as a Bäcker or an Apotheke are often close to a Haltestelle, so you can do errands on foot. Public transport timetables are often very precise, and people like to be on time when they meet a friend at a stop.

intro.title: Possessive articles: mein, dein, sein, ihr
explanation: A possessive article shows who something belongs to: mein Bus (my bus), dein Park (your park). The stem depends on the owner: ich = mein, du = dein, er/es = sein, sie = ihr, wir = unser, ihr = euer, Sie = Ihr.
The ending depends on the noun that follows: its gender, its number and its case. The endings are the same as for ein/eine/ein (and kein): mein Bahnhof, meine Straße, mein Haus, meine Freunde.

In the nominative (the subject) the masculine and neuter forms have no ending. In the accusative (the direct object) only the masculine changes: Ich sehe meinen Bahnhof. In the dative (after mit, bei, zu, in for where?) the endings are -em, -er, -em, -en: mit meinem Bus, mit meiner Freundin.
In the dative plural the noun also usually gets -n: bei meinen Eltern. Remember: sein = his, ihr = her. The owner decides the stem, not the noun.
intro.rule_summary: Stem = owner (mein, dein, sein, ihr); ending = noun's gender and case, like ein: Nom mein/meine/mein, Akk meinen/meine/mein, Dat meinem/meiner/meinem.

pronunciation.focus: ei and eu in mein, dein, sein and Freund
pronunciation.explanation: The letters ei sound like English "eye": mein, dein, sein. The letters eu sound like English "oy": Freund. Do not read ei like English "ee".

words.hint: m + ei + n: sounds like English "mine".

F + r + eu + n + d: eu sounds like "oy", so "froynt".

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: Pronouns in the accusative and dative: ihn, ihm, mich, mir ...
explanation: When you ask for or give directions, you often talk about people: 'Can you help me?', 'I show you the way', 'I don't see him'. The pronoun changes depending on the verb. After some verbs it is accusative (mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie, Sie). After others it is dative (mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen).

Most verbs take the accusative: sehen, fragen, brauchen, suchen, kennen. A few common verbs take the dative: helfen, danken, gehören. Learn them as pairs: 'helfen + dative', 'fragen + accusative'. Prepositions also matter: mit always takes the dative (mit dir, mit ihm).

With zeigen you have both: the person is dative and the thing is accusative: 'Ich zeige dir den Weg.' Only uns, euch, sie (they) and Sie keep the same form in the accusative as in other cases or the nominative; always check the table.
original.rule_summary: Accusative: mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie, Sie. Dative: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen. Learn helfen, danken and mit with the dative.

items.reason: The claim that only uns, euch, sie and Sie keep the same form was false (es and sie 'she' do too). Rewrote that sentence accurately.

final.title: Pronouns in the accusative and dative: ihn, ihm, mich, mir ...
explanation: When you ask for or give directions, you often talk about people: 'Can you help me?', 'I show you the way', 'I don't see him'. The pronoun changes depending on the verb. After some verbs it is accusative (mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie, Sie). After others it is dative (mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen).

Most verbs take the accusative: sehen, fragen, brauchen, suchen, kennen. A few common verbs take the dative: helfen, danken, gehören. Learn them as pairs: 'helfen + dative', 'fragen + accusative'. Prepositions also matter: mit always takes the dative (mit dir, mit ihm).

With zeigen you have both: the person is dative and the thing is accusative: 'Ich zeige dir den Weg.' Some forms look the same in two cases: sie, es, sie (they) and Sie are the same in the nominative and accusative, and uns and euch are the same in the accusative and dative. Always check the table.

original.title: Asking for directions in German-speaking countries
original.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people are usually happy to help if you ask politely. Start with "Entschuldigung" and use "Sie" with adults you do not know. Many people will explain the way with "geradeaus", "links" and "rechts", and often name landmarks such as a traffic light (die Ampel) or a crossing (die Kreuzung). Street signs show the street name on the corner of buildings. Many towns have a train station (der Bahnhof) near the centre, and it is a good starting point for directions. Most people also use a map app on their phone, but asking a person is still normal and friendly. At the end, say "Vielen Dank für Ihre Hilfe."

intro.title: Pronouns in the accusative and dative: ihn, ihm, mich, mir ...
explanation: When you ask for or give directions, you often talk about people: 'Can you help me?', 'I show you the way', 'I don't see him'. The pronoun changes depending on the verb. After some verbs it is accusative (mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie, Sie). After others it is dative (mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen).

Most verbs take the accusative: sehen, fragen, brauchen, suchen, kennen. A few common verbs take the dative: helfen, danken, gehören. Learn them as pairs: 'helfen + dative', 'fragen + accusative'. Prepositions also matter: mit always takes the dative (mit dir, mit ihm).

With zeigen you have both: the person is dative and the thing is accusative: 'Ich zeige dir den Weg.' Some forms look the same in two cases: sie, es, sie (they) and Sie are the same in the nominative and accusative, and uns and euch are the same in the accusative and dative. Always check the table.
intro.rule_summary: Accusative: mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie, Sie. Dative: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen. Learn helfen, danken and mit with the dative.

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: The imperative: telling someone what to do (du / ihr / Sie)
explanation: German has three imperative forms, depending on who you talk to. For du, take the verb stem (the infinitive without -en): kommen becomes Komm! For ihr, use the ihr form of the verb without the word ihr: Kommt! For the formal Sie, put the verb first and keep Sie: Kommen Sie!
Some verbs change their vowel in the du-form (e to i): sprechen becomes Sprich!, lesen becomes Lies!. The verb sein is irregular: Sei pünktlich! / Seid pünktlich! / Seien Sie pünktlich!
Separable verbs put the prefix at the end: anrufen becomes Ruf mich an! / Ruft mich an! / Rufen Sie mich an! Add bitte to be polite: Warte bitte kurz.
original.rule_summary: du: stem (Komm!) · ihr: ihr-form without ihr (Kommt!) · Sie: infinitive + Sie (Kommen Sie!); sein: Sei / Seid / Seien Sie.

original.title: Being on time in German-speaking countries
original.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, being on time is usually seen as a sign of respect. For a doctor's appointment, a meeting at work or a train, people try to arrive a few minutes early. If you will be late, it is polite to call or write a message before the appointment. In daily life, people often say a time like "um halb drei". Careful: halb drei means 2:30, not 3:30, because it is half an hour before three. Many people also use the 24-hour clock in writing and official announcements, for example 14:30 on a train timetable, but in speech they often say "halb drei". Among friends, a small delay of a few minutes can be fine at a private party, but for appointments it is better to be punctual.

intro.title: The imperative: telling someone what to do (du / ihr / Sie)
explanation: German has three imperative forms, depending on who you talk to. For du, take the verb stem (the infinitive without -en): kommen becomes Komm! For ihr, use the ihr form of the verb without the word ihr: Kommt! For the formal Sie, put the verb first and keep Sie: Kommen Sie!
Some verbs change their vowel in the du-form (e to i or ie): sprechen becomes Sprich!, lesen becomes Lies!. The verb sein is irregular: Sei pünktlich! / Seid pünktlich! / Seien Sie pünktlich!
Separable verbs put the prefix at the end: anrufen becomes Ruf mich an! / Ruft mich an! / Rufen Sie mich an! Add bitte to be polite: Warte bitte kurz.
intro.rule_summary: du: stem (Komm!) · ihr: ihr-form without ihr (Kommt!) · Sie: infinitive + Sie (Kommen Sie!); sein: Sei / Seid / Seien Sie.

culture.title: Being on time in German-speaking countries
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, being on time is usually seen as a sign of respect. For a doctor's appointment, a meeting at work or a train, people try to arrive a few minutes early. If you will be late, it is polite to call or write a message before the appointment. In daily life, people often say a time like "um halb drei". Careful: halb drei means 2:30, not 3:30, because it is half an hour before three. Many people also use the 24-hour clock in writing and official announcements, for example 14:30 on a train timetable, but in speech they often say "halb drei". Among friends, a small delay of a few minutes can be fine at a private party, but for appointments it is better to be punctual.

original.title: Perfekt with haben: talking about the weekend
explanation: In spoken German you usually talk about the past with the Perfekt. It has two parts: a form of haben (ich habe, du hast, er hat ...) in second position, and the Partizip II (past participle) at the very end of the sentence.

Regular verbs build the Partizip II with ge- + stem + -t: spielen → gespielt, kochen → gekocht. Verbs with a vowel change or other irregularities usually use ge- + stem + -en: sehen → gesehen, schlafen → geschlafen. You have to learn these participles with the verb.
If the stem ends in -t, add -et: arbeiten → gearbeitet. Time words such as am Samstag can start the sentence; haben still stays in second position and the participle stays at the end.
original.rule_summary: Perfekt with haben = haben (position 2) + ... + ge-...-t / ge-...-en (at the end).

original.focus: The ge- of the Partizip II and the sounds sp, sch and ch inside participles
original.explanation: The prefix ge- is short and weak, like the first syllable of English "gutter" without the stress: the g is hard and the e is like a quick "uh". The stress stays on the stem. At the start of a stem, sp sounds like "shp" (gespielt), sch sounds like English "sh" (geschlafen), and ch after o or au sounds like a rough breath in the throat (gekocht).

guh-LAIRNT: the stress is on lernt.
guh-HURT: ö is like the vowel in English "hurt", with rounded lips.
guh-TROON-ken: u is short and tr is clear.

original.title: The weekend in Germany
original.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, Sunday is a quiet day. Most shops, supermarkets and many other businesses are closed on Sundays, so people often buy what they need on Saturday. On Sunday many people go for a walk in a park, meet friends or family for coffee and cake (Kaffee und Kuchen), or cook a big meal at home. Many people also play sports. Football clubs, for example, often play their games on the weekend. Because of the Sunday quiet, many people plan their weekend: Saturday for shopping and errands, Sunday for rest. Cafés, cinemas and restaurants are usually open, so they are popular places on Sunday.

intro.title: Perfekt with haben: talking about the weekend
explanation: In spoken German you usually talk about the past with the Perfekt. It has two parts: a form of haben (ich habe, du hast, er hat ...) in second position, and the Partizip II (past participle) at the very end of the sentence.

Regular verbs build the Partizip II with ge- + stem + -t: spielen → gespielt, kochen → gekocht. Verbs with a vowel change or other irregularities usually use ge- + stem + -en: sehen → gesehen, schlafen → geschlafen. You have to learn these participles with the verb.
If the stem ends in -t, add -et: arbeiten → gearbeitet. Time words such as am Samstag can start the sentence; haben still stays in second position and the participle stays at the end.
intro.rule_summary: Perfekt with haben = haben (position 2) + ... + ge-...-t / ge-...-en (at the end).

pronunciation.focus: The ge- of the Partizip II and the sounds sp, sch and ch inside participles
pronunciation.explanation: The prefix ge- is short and weak, like the first syllable of English "gutter" without the stress: the g is hard and the e is like a quick "uh". The stress stays on the stem. At the start of a stem, sp sounds like "shp" (gespielt), sch sounds like English "sh" (geschlafen), and ch after o or au sounds like a rough breath in the throat (gekocht).

words.hint: guh-SHPEELT: s + p at the start of the stem sounds like "shp".
guh-KOCHT: the ch comes after o, a breathy sound from the throat.
guh-ZAY-en: the h is silent and only makes the e long.
guh-LAIRNT: the stress is on lernt.
guh-HURT: ö is like the vowel in English "hurt", with rounded lips.
guh-TROON-ken: u is short and tr is clear.

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: Perfekt with sein: where did you go?
explanation: To talk about the past in everyday German, we use the Perfekt. It has two parts: a helping verb (haben or sein) in position 2 and a past participle at the very end of the sentence.

Verbs that show a change of place (gehen, fahren, laufen, fliegen, kommen) use sein as the helping verb. Two other important verbs also use sein: bleiben (to stay) and sein (to be). Most other verbs use haben.

The participle of many of these verbs starts with ge- and ends in -en: gegangen, gefahren, geflogen. Learn each participle together with the verb, because the middle of the word often changes (gehen, gegangen).
original.rule_summary: Perfekt with sein = form of sein (position 2) + past participle (at the end): Ich bin ins Kino gegangen.

items.reason: Accurate explanation of the Perfekt with sein.

original.title: Free time in Germany: Vereine and the weekend
original.note: Many people in Germany spend their free time in a Verein, which is a club. There are clubs for football, music, swimming, cycling and many other hobbies. People often meet there once or twice a week. On Sundays most shops are closed, so the weekend is a quiet time. Many people go for a walk in the park, take a bike ride to a lake, visit a museum or meet friends in a café. In summer, lakes and outdoor pools (Freibäder) are popular. Many families also plan a short Ausflug on a Saturday or Sunday. Of course, not everybody does the same thing: some people just stay at home and relax.
original.reflection_question: What do you usually do on the weekend, and where do people in your country go in their free time?

intro.title: Perfekt with sein: where did you go?
explanation: To talk about the past in everyday German, we use the Perfekt. It has two parts: a helping verb (haben or sein) in position 2 and a past participle at the very end of the sentence.

Verbs that show a change of place (gehen, fahren, laufen, fliegen, kommen) use sein as the helping verb. Two other important verbs also use sein: bleiben (to stay) and sein (to be). Most other verbs use haben.

The participle of many of these verbs starts with ge- and ends in -en: gegangen, gefahren, geflogen. Learn each participle together with the verb, because the middle of the word often changes (gehen, gegangen).
intro.rule_summary: Perfekt with sein = form of sein (position 2) + past participle (at the end): Ich bin ins Kino gegangen.

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: Irregular Partizip II: the 40 verbs you need for travel stories
explanation: You already know the Perfekt: a form of haben or sein in second position, and the Partizip II at the end of the sentence. Regular verbs end in -t (gemacht). Many very common verbs are irregular. Their Partizip II usually ends in -en (gesehen, gefahren), and often the vowel in the stem changes (trinken, getrunken). You have to learn these forms by heart.

Most irregular verbs form the Perfekt with haben: Ich habe ein Buch gelesen. Verbs of movement or change of place (fahren, fliegen, gehen, kommen) and the verbs sein and bleiben use sein: Wir sind nach Rom geflogen. The forms of the verb are the same as for the regular ones, only the Partizip II is new.

A small group of mixed verbs has the regular ending -t but also changes its stem: bringen, gebracht. Learn them as a separate group. Verbs with a separable prefix put ge- in the middle: ankommen, angekommen; einsteigen, eingestiegen. The verb bekommen and the verb beginnen have no ge-: bekommen, begonnen.
original.rule_summary: haben/sein + Partizip II at the end; irregular Partizip II usually ends in -en with a changed stem (gesehen, gefahren); movement verbs, sein and bleiben take sein.

items.reason: Accurate explanation; the 40 verbs match the tables.

intro.title: Irregular Partizip II: the 40 verbs you need for travel stories
explanation: You already know the Perfekt: a form of haben or sein in second position, and the Partizip II at the end of the sentence. Regular verbs end in -t (gemacht). Many very common verbs are irregular. Their Partizip II usually ends in -en (gesehen, gefahren), and often the vowel in the stem changes (trinken, getrunken). You have to learn these forms by heart.

Most irregular verbs form the Perfekt with haben: Ich habe ein Buch gelesen. Verbs of movement or change of place (fahren, fliegen, gehen, kommen) and the verbs sein and bleiben use sein: Wir sind nach Rom geflogen. The forms of the verb are the same as for the regular ones, only the Partizip II is new.

A small group of mixed verbs has the regular ending -t but also changes its stem: bringen, gebracht. Learn them as a separate group. Verbs with a separable prefix put ge- in the middle: ankommen, angekommen; einsteigen, eingestiegen. The verb bekommen and the verb beginnen have no ge-: bekommen, begonnen.
intro.rule_summary: haben/sein + Partizip II at the end; irregular Partizip II usually ends in -en with a changed stem (gesehen, gefahren); movement verbs, sein and bleiben take sein.

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: Perfekt with separable and inseparable verbs
explanation: The Perfekt has two parts: haben (or sein) in second position and the participle (Partizip II) at the end. Regular verbs form the participle as ge- + stem + -t: arbeiten → gearbeitet.
Separable verbs have a prefix such as an-, auf-, ein-, mit- or ab-. In the participle, ge- goes between the prefix and the verb: anrufen → angerufen, aufräumen → aufgeräumt, einkaufen → eingekauft.
Inseparable verbs start with be-, ver-, er-, ent- or zer-. They get no ge- at all: besuchen → besucht, verstehen → verstanden, bekommen → bekommen.
Most verbs use haben. Verbs of movement or change of place or state, such as ankommen, aufstehen and mitkommen, use sein: Lena ist angekommen.
original.rule_summary: Separable: prefix + ge + stem (angerufen); inseparable: no ge- (besucht); most verbs take haben, movement verbs like ankommen take sein.

items.reason: Accurate explanation of participle formation and the auxiliaries.

final.title: Perfekt with separable and inseparable verbs
explanation: The Perfekt has two parts: haben (or sein) in second position and the participle (Partizip II) at the end. Regular verbs form the participle as ge- + stem + -t: arbeiten → gearbeitet.

Inseparable verbs start with be-, ver-, er-, ent- or zer-. They get no ge- at all: besuchen → besucht, verstehen → verstanden, bekommen → bekommen.

items.label: Pronunciation focus

original.focus: Stress in separable and inseparable verbs
original.explanation: In separable verbs the stress is on the prefix: AN-gerufen. In inseparable verbs the prefix is unstressed and the stress falls on the stem: be-SUCHT. The unstressed ge- and be- are short and weak.

words.hint: AUF-ge-räumt: stress AUF; äu sounds like English oy.
EIN-ge-kauft: stress EIN, which sounds like English eye-n.
be-SUCHT: stress the second syllable; ch as in Bach.
fer-SHTAN-den: stress STAN; v sounds like f, st like sht.
be-ZAHLT: stress ZAHLT; z sounds like ts and ah is long.

original.title: Working hours and punctuality in German-speaking countries
original.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, being on time at work is very important. If you have an appointment (ein Termin) or a meeting (eine Besprechung), you usually arrive a few minutes early. If you are going to be late, you call or write an e-mail and say so. Many offices also offer flexible working hours, but a fixed time for meetings is still normal. Colleagues often greet each other in the morning with Guten Morgen or Hallo. In many companies, colleagues use du with each other, but with customers and with the boss people often use Sie. If you are not sure, start with Sie. Breaks are also common: many people take a short break for lunch or coffee with colleagues.

intro.title: Perfekt with separable and inseparable verbs
explanation: The Perfekt has two parts: haben (or sein) in second position and the participle (Partizip II) at the end. Regular verbs form the participle as ge- + stem + -t: arbeiten → gearbeitet.
Separable verbs have a prefix such as an-, auf-, ein-, mit- or ab-. In the participle, ge- goes between the prefix and the verb: anrufen → angerufen, aufräumen → aufgeräumt, einkaufen → eingekauft.
Inseparable verbs start with be-, ver-, er-, ent- or zer-. They get no ge- at all: besuchen → besucht, verstehen → verstanden, bekommen → bekommen.
Most verbs use haben. Verbs of movement or change of place or state, such as ankommen, aufstehen and mitkommen, use sein: Lena ist angekommen.
intro.rule_summary: Separable: prefix + ge + stem (angerufen); inseparable: no ge- (besucht); most verbs take haben, movement verbs like ankommen take sein.

pronunciation.focus: Stress in separable and inseparable verbs
pronunciation.explanation: In separable verbs the stress is on the prefix: AN-gerufen. In inseparable verbs the prefix is unstressed and the stress falls on the stem: be-SUCHT. The unstressed ge- and be- are short and weak.

words.hint: AUF-ge-räumt: stress AUF; äu sounds like English oy.
EIN-ge-kauft: stress EIN, which sounds like English eye-n.
be-SUCHT: stress the second syllable; ch as in Bach.
fer-SHTAN-den: stress STAN; v sounds like f, st like sht.
be-ZAHLT: stress ZAHLT; z sounds like ts and ah is long.

original.title: Time expressions: am, um, im, seit, vor
explanation: German uses small words to say when something happens. Use am with days, dates and parts of the day (am Samstag, am 5. Mai, am Abend). Use um with clock times (um acht Uhr). Use im with months and seasons (im Mai, im Sommer).
Use seit for something that started in the past and is still true now: Ich wohne seit einem Jahr hier. Use vor for something that happened a certain time ago: Die Party war vor einer Woche.

After seit and vor the next word changes: einem Jahr, einer Woche, zwei Tagen. Learn these as fixed chunks at A1: seit einem Jahr, seit einer Woche, vor einem Jahr, vor einer Woche, vor zwei Tagen. With a day or month there is no change: seit Montag, seit Juni.
original.rule_summary: am = day, date, part of the day; um = clock time; im = month, season; seit = since / for (still going on); vor = ago.

Use seit for something that started in the past and is still true now: Ich wohne seit einem Jahr hier. Use vor for something that happened a certain time ago: Die Party war vor einer Woche.

After seit and vor the next word changes: einem Jahr, einer Woche, zwei Tagen. Learn these as fixed chunks at A1: seit einem Jahr, seit einer Woche, vor einem Jahr, vor einer Woche, vor zwei Tagen. With a day or month there is no change: seit Montag, seit Juni.

intro.title: Time expressions: am, um, im, seit, vor
explanation: German uses small words to say when something happens. Use am with days, dates and parts of the day (am Samstag, am 5. Mai, am Abend). Use um with clock times (um acht Uhr). Use im with months and seasons (im Mai, im Sommer).
Use seit for something that started in the past and is still true now: Ich wohne seit einem Jahr hier. Use vor for something that happened a certain time ago: Die Party war vor einer Woche.

After seit and vor the next word changes: einem Jahr, einer Woche, zwei Tagen. Learn these as fixed chunks at A1: seit einem Jahr, seit einer Woche, vor einem Jahr, vor einer Woche, vor zwei Tagen. With a day or month there is no change: seit Montag, seit Juni.
intro.rule_summary: am = day, date, part of the day; um = clock time; im = month, season; seit = since / for (still going on); vor = ago.

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: Prepositions with the accusative: für, durch, ohne, gegen, um
explanation: Some German prepositions are always followed by the accusative case. Five important ones are für (for), durch (through), ohne (without), gegen (against, into) and um (around). You never have to think about 'where' or 'whether something moves'; these five always take the accusative.
In the accusative only the masculine nouns change: der becomes den and ein becomes einen. Feminine, neuter and plural nouns look the same as in the nominative: die Lampe, das Bett, die Stühle.
After ohne you often use no article at all when you mean 'without any': ohne Kissen. If you want to say 'without the pillow', use ohne das Kissen.
original.rule_summary: für, durch, ohne, gegen, um + accusative: der → den, ein → einen; die, das and plural stay the same.

original.title: Living in a German-speaking country: rooms and furniture
original.note: Many people in Germany, Austria and Switzerland rent their home instead of buying it. Rented flats are often unfurnished. Sometimes there is not even a kitchen, so tenants bring their own Küche, lamps and Schränke. Because of this, many people take their furniture with them when they move. Flats are often described by the number of rooms, such as a Zwei-Zimmer-Wohnung. Kitchen and bathroom are usually not counted. Many people also open the window wide for a few minutes every day to let in fresh air. Used furniture is popular too, and people sell or give away things like a Sessel, a Regal or a Tisch to others.

intro.title: Prepositions with the accusative: für, durch, ohne, gegen, um
explanation: Some German prepositions are always followed by the accusative case. Five important ones are für (for), durch (through), ohne (without), gegen (against, into) and um (around). You never have to think about 'where' or 'whether something moves'; these five always take the accusative.
In the accusative only the masculine nouns change: der becomes den and ein becomes einen. Feminine, neuter and plural nouns look the same as in the nominative: die Lampe, das Bett, die Stühle.
After ohne you often use no article at all when you mean 'without any': ohne Kissen. If you want to say 'without the pillow', use ohne das Kissen.
intro.rule_summary: für, durch, ohne, gegen, um + accusative: der → den, ein → einen; die, das and plural stay the same.

culture.title: Living in a German-speaking country: rooms and furniture
culture.note: Many people in Germany, Austria and Switzerland rent their home instead of buying it. Rented flats are often unfurnished. Sometimes there is not even a kitchen, so tenants bring their own Küche, lamps and Schränke. Because of this, many people take their furniture with them when they move. Flats are often described by the number of rooms, such as a Zwei-Zimmer-Wohnung. Kitchen and bathroom are usually not counted. Many people also open the window wide for a few minutes every day to let in fresh air. Used furniture is popular too, and people sell or give away things like a Sessel, a Regal or a Tisch to others.

items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: Seven prepositions that always take the Dativ
explanation: The prepositions aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von and zu are always followed by the dative case. This is true every time, so you do not have to decide: after these words, use the dative.

In the dative, der and das become dem, die becomes der, and the plural becomes den (and the noun usually adds -n): mit dem Auto, bei der Nachbarin, mit den Nachbarn. The indefinite articles are einem (der/das) and einer (die).
Some prepositions merge with the article: zu + dem = zum, zu + der = zur, von + dem = vom, bei + dem = beim. Use these in everyday speech.
Use nach for cities and countries (nach Berlin) and in nach Hause (going home). Use zu Hause for being at home. Use zu for going to a person or a place (zur Wohnung, zum Nachbarn).
original.rule_summary: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu + Dativ: dem (der/das), der (die), den + -n (plural); zum, zur, vom, beim are short forms.
